meta.note: Original texts, English translations and source metadata for the atlas. Russian originals retain the orthography of the cited edition. Translations are the atlas's own unless stated otherwise. Every complete text reproduced here is public domain; see RIGHTS_CLEARANCE_LOG.md.

voices.title: A widow's lament for her husband (opening)
voices.performer_note: Barsov identifies Fedosova, of Kuzaranda in Zaonezhye, as the performer of laments I, IV, VI–X, XIII–XVII and XX–XXIII in volume 1. He recorded her in Petrozavodsk in 1867–68.
voices.rights_evidence: Barsov died in 1917; the volume was published in 1872. The text is public domain in Russia (70 years p.m.a.) and in the United States (published before 1929). The transcription was checked line by line against the Internet Archive scan of the 1872 edition.
voices.source_detail: E. V. Barsov, Prichitaniya Severnogo kraia, vol. 1 (Moscow, 1872), p. 1, lines 1–15.
voices.excerpt_note: Lines 1–15 of a lament that continues for several pages. The excerpt stops before a dialect form that Barsov does not gloss.
original: За горы оно да за высокія,
За лѣсушка оно да за дремучіи,
За облачка оно да за ходячіи,
Со стадушкомъ оно да со дѣтиною;
Будутъ по міру оны да вѣдь скитатися,
Путь дорожинька вотъ имъ да не торнешенька:
translation: The red sun has rolled away
Beyond the mountains, beyond the high ones,
Beyond the forests, beyond the dense ones,
Beyond the clouds, beyond the wandering ones,
Beyond the frequent stars, the eastern ones!
He is leaving me, a poor woman,
With his little flock, with his children;
He is abandoning me, a grieving woman,
For all ages, for ever and ever!
How am I to raise the orphaned children?
They will wander through the world,
They will knock at strangers' windows;
The street they walk will not be wide,
The path before them will not be trodden:
Without their parent, without their father…
context: Barsov prints this as the first lament in the collection. It opens not with the deathbed but with the sun going down behind mountains, forests, clouds and stars; the dead man's departure is described as a cosmic disappearance before it is described as a household loss. The second movement turns to the widow's children: they will wander, knock at strangers' windows, and walk a road that is not wide or trodden. The formula «победная головушка» (poor, wretched woman) is a genre marker, not a personal epithet.

Fedosova dictated her laments to Barsov in Petrozavodsk in 1867–68. Barsov notes that she dictated slowly and that he wrote down each word; the text is a transcription of a repertoire, not a recording of a funeral. The atlas prints the first fifteen lines. The following line in the printed text contains a dialect form whose sense is not certain, and the excerpt stops before it.

notes.gloss: Formulaic self-designation: the poor, wretched woman. Not a literal reference to the head.
A grieving woman; a genre term for the mourner.
Little flock; a collective image for the children.
Collective form: the children, the little ones. Barsov’s own footnote on this word: used here in a collective sense.
Barsov’s own footnote on line 12 glosses it as ‘to wander in crowds’ (толпами бродить).

voices.title: A lament for a sister
voices.place: Selo Tverdilovo, Kalyazin uyezd, Tver province
voices.performer_note: Barsov's register of performers (vol. 1, pp. 326–327) identifies her: a peasant of Selo Tverdilovo, Kalyazin uyezd, Tver province; she learned to lament in her village as a girl; she married a widower, lived with him twelve years and had been widowed six years when Barsov wrote; four daughters were born, one survived; she was then living in Moscow. Barsov records that Lament XI was taken from her.
voices.rights_evidence: Barsov died in 1917; the volume was published in 1872. Public domain in Russia and in the United States. The transcription was checked line by line against the Internet Archive scan, pp. 162–164.
voices.source_detail: E. V. Barsov, Prichitaniya Severnogo kraia, vol. 1 (Moscow, 1872), pp. 162–164, no. XI, lines 1–42.
original: Ты во снѣ нонь не покажешься
translation: Little dove, my dear sister!
Where have you gone and arrayed yourself,
Where have you gone and made yourself ready?
On what road, on what pathway,
To what guests, unknown,
Unknown and unwanted?
You have arrayed yourself, made yourself ready
For eternal life, without end.
Without you, my dear sister,
Now everything here is empty, quite empty,
The wide tower has grown empty,
In the wide courtyard;
Without you, my dear sister,
I am no worker, no labourer,
I take upon myself every kind of thing,
Both cold and hunger
And great reproach;
Little dove, my dear sister!
You will not call out to me, will not speak to me,
You will not appear to me in a dream,
You will not show yourself to me awake;
I have lost my firm thought,
A secret word—not to be carried abroad,
And my great protection.
Rise up, you wild winds,
With your fine little whirlwinds!
Scatter the yellow sands,
The yellow sands—the small stones!
Open up, mother moist earth,
Open, coffin lid,
Unfold, fine white shroud!
Lift up, my dear sister,
Your bright eyes
Stand up, my dear sister,
On your swift little legs
Fly up as a small bird
To your own warm nest;
Let us come together, close, very close
Let us bow low, very low
Let us think and take counsel
How I am to pass my maiden's life
Do not let me languish long.
context: This is one of the few complete laments in Barsov's first volume. It was recorded in Kalyazin uyezd, Tver province, not in the Olonets North, and printed as No. XI. Barsov's register of performers (pp. 326–327) identifies the performer as Klavdiya Momokova, a peasant of Selo Tverdilovo; she learned to lament in the village as a girl and was living in Moscow when Barsov wrote. The text is short enough to print in full.

The sister's lament moves from the dead woman's departure to «unknown guests» to the emptiness of the house, the survivor's loss of a «secret word» and «protection», and then to the invocation of wind, earth, coffin lid and shroud. The request that the dead sister rise and speak is a conventional motif. The closing line asks not for resurrection but for the grief to be shortened. The text is printed in the original pre-1918 orthography; line breaks and repetitions are retained. After the last line Barsov prints a footnote with a variant of about twenty lines for the passage on the winds, the earth and the shroud; the variant is not reproduced here.

notes.gloss: Arrayed herself, made herself ready; the verbs belong to the ritual language of departure.
The upper room or tower of a house; here the whole household.
Protection, intercession; the sister was the mourner's defender.
To languish, to suffer without relief.

voices.title: Lament for the drowned (excerpt)
voices.genre: Funeral lament for the unburied dead
voices.performer_note: No. XVII in volume 1. Barsov lists it among the laments recorded from Fedosova.
voices.rights_evidence: Barsov died in 1917; the volume was published in 1872. Public domain in Russia and in the United States. The transcription was checked line by line against the Internet Archive scan, pp. 258–259.
voices.source_detail: E. V. Barsov, Prichitaniya Severnogo kraia, vol. 1 (Moscow, 1872), pp. 252–259, no. XVII, lines 175–192.
voices.excerpt_note: Lines 175–192 of a lament of more than 220 lines. The excerpt stops before a dialect verb whose sense is uncertain.
original: Тѣлеса у ихъ пойдутъ безъ погребенія,
Не приданы ко матушкѣ сырой землѣ;
Не умершей мы ихной тамъ могилушки!
Лучше далъ бы Господь скорую смерётушку,
На своей бѣлой, брусовой имъ на лавочкѣ,
Во своемъ домѣ крестьянской-бы во жирушкѣ;
Мы поповъ отцевъ вѣдь тутъ да попросили-бы,
Въ Божью церковь посвященну мы сносили-бы,
translation: Do the dogs not drag their bones?
In grave sins—without repentance,
They have received an untimely death;
Their bodies will lie without burial,
Not given over to mother moist earth;
The wild wind will wrap them,
The red sun will warm them,
Snow will fall on the body like feathered down;
We do not know, poor wretches—
We do not know their grave, where they lie dead!
Better would the Lord have given a swift death,
On their own white, hewn bench,
In their own peasant household;
Then we would have summoned the priests, the spiritual fathers,
We would have carried them to God's holy church,
We would have buried them with honour and name;
We would know where the grave of the dead lies,
We would go there on the Lord's holy feast.
context: The lament is spoken by a daughter who survived a storm on Lake Onega; her father and brother drowned. In this passage she describes what happens to those who die without confession and without burial: their bodies are not given to the earth, the wind wraps them, the sun warms them, snow falls on them, and the family has no grave to visit. The passage contrasts this death with the good death at home, on one's own bench, with priests and burial.

The text is No. XVII in Barsov's first volume and comes from Fedosova's repertoire. Barsov prints the full lament, which includes the storm, the survival and the search for the bodies. The atlas prints lines 175–192 only. The following line contains a dialect verb whose sense is uncertain, and the excerpt stops before it.

notes.gloss: Death, in a diminutive form; the lament uses affectionate diminutives even for death.
Poor wretch; a formula of self-pity, not a literal head.
Given over, consigned; here, to the earth.
Household, dwelling, the peasant home with its stores.
Printed form of a dialect verb; the sense is not certain. Translated tentatively as ‘will wrap’.

voices.title: On the Death of Prince Meshchersky
voices.author: Gavriil Romanovich Derzhavin (1743–1816)
voices.language: Russian (modern orthography, following the cited edition)
voices.rights_evidence: Derzhavin died in 1816; the ode was published in 1779. Public domain in Russia and in the United States. The text follows the Wikisource transcription based on Dukhovnye ody (1993) and was checked against the cited edition's lineation.
voices.source_detail: G. R. Derzhavin, «На смерть князя Мещерского» (1779), lines 1–16.
voices.excerpt_note: Lines 1–16 of an ode of 88 lines. The excerpt is the opening; the poem continues with the death of Meshchersky and the consolation of Perfilyev.
original: И дни мои, как злак, сечет.
Как в море льются быстры воды,
Так в вечность льются дни и годы;
translation: The word of times! The clang of metal!
Your terrible voice confounds me;
Your groan calls me, calls me,
Calls—and brings me nearer to the grave.
Scarcely had I seen this light
When death already gnashes its teeth,
Flashes its scythe like lightning,
And cuts my days like grass.
Nothing escapes the fatal claws,
No creature flees them;
Monarch and prisoner are food for worms,
The fury of the elements devours tombs;
Time gapes to wipe away glory:
As swift waters flow into the sea,
So days and years flow into eternity;
Greedy death swallows kingdoms.
context: Derzhavin wrote the ode in 1779 on the death of Prince Aleksandr Ivanovich Meshchersky (1713–1779), a courtier and friend. It is not a funeral lament and was not performed at a funeral. It is a literary meditation on time, death and the vanity of rank, written for the court and the printed page.

The opening turns the sound of a clock into the voice of time and the approach of the grave. The images that follow—death as a reaper, the tomb as the leveler, the monarch and the prisoner as food for worms—belong to the eighteenth-century graveyard tradition and to Orthodox moral verse. The atlas prints the first sixteen lines; the poem continues for another seventy-two lines. It is evidence for elite literary culture, not for peasant ritual.

notes.gloss: The word or voice of the times; an archaic, biblical phrase.
The ringing of metal; most likely a clock, whose sound becomes the voice of time.
Food for worms; a traditional memento mori image.

voices.title_ru: Брожу ли я вдоль улиц шумных…
voices.title: Whether I wander along noisy streets…
voices.first_line: Брожу ли я вдоль улиц шумных,
voices.place: Composed 1829; published in Literaturnaya gazeta, St Petersburg
voices.author: Alexander Sergeevich Pushkin (1799–1837)
voices.language: Russian (modern orthography, following the cited edition)
voices.rights_evidence: Pushkin died in 1837; the poem was published in 1830. Public domain in Russia and in the United States. The text follows the Wikisource transcription based on Sobranie sochinenii v 10 tomakh (1956–62).
voices.source_detail: A. S. Pushkin, «Брожу ли я вдоль улиц шумных…» (26 December 1829; published 6 January 1830), 32 lines.
original: Брожу ли я вдоль улиц шумных,
И сколько здесь ни видно нас,
Мы все сойдём под вечны своды —
И где мне смерть пошлёт судьбина?
В бою ли, в странствии, в волнах?
translation: Whether I wander along noisy streets,
Or enter a crowded church,
Or sit among mad youths,
I give myself up to my dreams.
I say: the years will rush by,
And however many of us are visible here,
We shall all go down beneath the eternal vaults—
And someone's hour is already near.
Whether I look at a solitary oak,
I think: the patriarch of the forests
Will outlive my forgotten age,
As he outlived the age of my fathers.
Whether I caress a dear infant,
I already think: farewell!
I yield my place to you:
It is time for me to decay, for you to bloom.
Every day, every year
I am accustomed to accompany with thought,
Trying to guess among them
The anniversary of my coming death.
And where will fate send death to me?
In battle, in wandering, in the waves?
Or will the neighboring valley
Receive my cooled ashes?
And though it is all the same to the insensible body
Where it decays,
Still, closer to my dear native place
I would like to rest.
And let young life play
At the entrance to the grave,
And let indifferent nature
Shine with eternal beauty.
context: Pushkin wrote the poem on 26 December 1829; it was published in Literaturnaya gazeta on 6 January 1830. It is a lyric meditation, not a funeral text. The speaker moves through a street, a church, a crowd of youths, an oak, an infant, and ends at the entrance to the grave, where young life continues and indifferent nature shines.

The poem is used in the plate on the grave because it states the grave as a place that is both personal («closer to my dear native place») and impersonal («it is all the same to the insensible body»). The «eternal vaults» are a literary image, not a description of a cemetery. The text follows the modern-spelling edition cited; the source page records the pre-reform variants.

notes.gloss: Limit, boundary, region; here rendered as «native place».
Eternal vaults; the grave or the underworld, a literary image.
Indifferent nature; the poem's final antithesis to human grief.

voices.title: I come out alone onto the road…
voices.author: Mikhail Yuryevich Lermontov (1814–1841)
voices.language: Russian (modern orthography, following the cited edition)
voices.rights_evidence: Lermontov died in 1841; the poem was published in 1843. Public domain in Russia and in the United States. The text follows the Wikisource transcription of Polnoe sobranie stikhotvorenii (1989), vol. 2, p. 83.
voices.source_detail: M. Yu. Lermontov, «Выхожу один я на дорогу…» (1841; published 1843), 20 lines.
original: Что же мне так больно и так трудно?
Жду ль чего? Жалею ли о чем?
Уж не жду от жизни ничего я,
И не жаль мне прошлого ничуть.
Я б хотел забыться и заснуть!
Но не тем холодным сном могилы...
Я б желал навеки так заснуть,
Чтоб в груди дремали жизни силы,
Чтоб, всю ночь, весь день мой слух лелея,
Про любовь мне сладкий голос пел,
translation: I come out alone onto the road;
Through the mist the flinty path gleams.
The night is still. The wilderness hearkens to God,
And star speaks to star.
In the heavens it is solemn and wondrous!
The earth sleeps in a blue radiance...
Why is it so painful and so hard for me?
Am I waiting for something? Do I regret anything?
I no longer expect anything from life,
And I do not regret the past at all.
I seek freedom and peace!
I would like to forget myself and fall asleep!
But not with that cold sleep of the grave...
I would like to fall asleep like that forever,
So that the powers of life might slumber in my breast,
So that, breathing, my chest might rise quietly,
So that, all night, all day, cherishing my hearing,
A sweet voice might sing to me of love,
So that above me, forever green,
The dark oak might bend and murmur.
context: Lermontov wrote the poem in 1841, the year of his death; it was published in Otechestvennye zapiski in 1843. It is a lyric meditation, not a funeral text. The speaker is alone on a flinty road at night; he no longer expects anything from life and seeks freedom and peace, but he explicitly rejects the «cold sleep of the grave» in favour of a living, dreaming sleep.

The poem is used in the plate on death in art because it imagines death as a threshold that is also a place of continuing life. The dark oak at the end is a literary image, not a cemetery custom. The text follows the 1989 edition cited.

notes.gloss: A path of flint or gravel; the road is hard and bare.
Wilderness, emptiness; not a sandy desert.
To forget oneself and fall asleep; the poem distinguishes this from the sleep of death.

voices.title: Hearing the horrors of war…
voices.author: Nikolai Alekseevich Nekrasov (1821–1877)
voices.language: Russian (modern orthography, following the cited edition)
voices.rights_evidence: Nekrasov died in 1877; the poem was published in 1856. Public domain in Russia and in the United States. The text follows the Wikisource transcription of Polnoe sobranie sochinenii i pisem (1981–2000), vol. 2.
voices.source_detail: N. A. Nekrasov, «Внимая ужасам войны…» (1855; published 1856), 17 lines.
original: Мне жаль не друга, не жены,
translation: Hearing the horrors of war,
At each new victim of battle,
I grieve not for the friend, not for the wife,
I grieve not for the hero himself...
Alas! the wife will be comforted,
And the friend will be forgotten by his best friend;
But somewhere there is one soul—
It will remember until the grave!
Amid our hypocritical deeds
And all the vulgarity and prose,
I have glimpsed in the world
One kind of holy, sincere tears—
The tears of poor mothers!
They cannot forget their children,
Perished on the bloody field,
As a weeping willow cannot lift
Its drooping branches...
context: Nekrasov wrote the poem in 1855, during the Crimean War, and published it in 1856. It is not a soldier's song or a funeral lament. It is a literary argument that the true grief of war belongs to mothers, whose tears cannot be consoled, while wives and friends forget.

The poem is used in the plate on collective death as a counter to the state's monumental memory. It insists on the one mourner who does not forget, and it compares her to a weeping willow that cannot lift its branches. The «bloody field» is a literary generalization; the poem gives no place, date or name.

notes.gloss: Weeping willow; the branches droop, and the tree cannot lift them.
Bloody field; literally a field of grain, used as a metaphor of battle.

voices.title: Frost, Red Nose (excerpt)
voices.place: Composed 1863–64; the poem is set in a Russian peasant village
voices.author: Nikolai Alekseevich Nekrasov (1821–1877)
voices.language: Russian (modern orthography, following the cited edition)
voices.rights_evidence: Nekrasov died in 1877; the poem was published in 1863–64. Public domain in Russia and in the United States. The text follows the Wikisource transcription of Polnoe sobranie sochinenii i pisem (1981–2000), vol. 4, part I, ch. VIII, lines 260–275.
voices.source_detail: N. A. Nekrasov, «Мороз, Красный нос» (1863–64), part I, ch. VIII, lines 260–275.
voices.excerpt_note: Lines 260–275 of the poem: the laying out of Prokl. The funeral lament that follows is Nekrasov's literary composition, not a recorded folk text.
translation: Slowly, gravely, sternly
The sad work was done:
No unnecessary word was spoken,
No tears were shown outwardly.
He has fallen asleep, having laboured in sweat!
He has fallen asleep, having worked for the earth!
He lies, untouched by care,
On the white pine table,
He lies motionless, stern,
With a burning candle at his head,
In a wide linen shirt
And new linden bast shoes.
His big, calloused hands,
Which had lifted so much labour,
His handsome face, untouched by torment—
And a beard down to his hands...
context: Frost, Red Nose (1863–64) is a narrative poem about the death of the peasant Prokl and the grief of his widow Daria. The excerpt describes the laying out of the body: the silence in the house, the candle at the head, the wide linen shirt, the new bast shoes, the calloused hands. Nekrasov drew on ethnographic material, and contemporaries read the poem as a picture of peasant life, but it is not a transcript of a ritual.

The poem's funeral lament, which follows this passage, is Nekrasov's literary composition. The atlas does not present it as a folk lament; for recorded laments, see Plate G. The excerpt is printed as a literary image of the ritual, not as evidence of what was said or done.

notes.gloss: A shirt of coarse linen; the dead man is dressed in clean, plain cloth.
Bast shoes, woven from linden bark; the new pair marks the seriousness of the preparation.
A candle at the head of the dead; a standard element of Orthodox laying out.

voices.title_ru: Надпись на надгробии А. В. Суворова
voices.title: Inscription on the tomb of A. V. Suvorov
voices.author: Attributed to Gavriil Romanovich Derzhavin
voices.rights_evidence: The inscription was carved in 1800. The text is a short factual phrase and is public domain in every relevant jurisdiction. The attribution to Derzhavin rests on the anecdote recorded in the commentary to Gnedich's poem; the inscription itself is treated as an object, not as a literary work.
voices.source_detail: Inscription on the tomb of A. V. Suvorov, Annunciation Church, Alexander Nevsky Lavra, St Petersburg, 1800.
translation: Here lies Suvorov.
context: Suvorov died in 1800 and was buried in the Annunciation Church of the Alexander Nevsky Lavra in St Petersburg. The slab carries only these three words. The attribution to Derzhavin rests on an anecdote recorded in the commentary to Nikolai Gnedich's poem «Inscription to Suvorov's Tomb»: Suvorov asked Derzhavin what epitaph he would write, and Derzhavin replied that three words were enough.

The original slab was later replaced by a longer one with titles, but Suvorov's wish prevailed and the simple inscription was restored. The atlas prints the inscription as an inscription, not as a poem. The exact history of the slab is summarized in the Lavra and museum notices cited.

notes.gloss: Here lies; the inscription is a complete sentence, not a fragment.

voices.title: Funeral sticheron: «I weep and lament…»
voices.place: Russian Orthodox funeral rite for the laity
voices.date_published: received text; attributed to John of Damascus (c. 676–749)
voices.author: John of Damascus (attrib.)
voices.rights_evidence: The text is a liturgical composition of the first millennium, received in the Slavonic funeral rite. It is public domain. The English translation is the atlas's own and is not taken from a modern Russian translation.
voices.source_detail: Funeral sticheron, Tone 8, in the Orthodox burial rite for the laity.
original: по образу Божию созданную нашу красоту,
Что сие еже о нас бысть таинство?
translation: I weep and lament
when I think of death,
and see lying in the tombs
our beauty, created in the image of God,
disfigured, without glory,
without form.
O wonder!
What is this mystery that has come upon us?
How have we been given over to corruption?
How have we been joined to death?
Truly, by the command of God,
as it is written,
who grants rest to the departed.
context: This sticheron, Tone 8, is sung in the Orthodox funeral rite for the laity. It is not a folk lament and was not composed for a village performance; it is the Church's own funeral language. The text is attributed to John of Damascus (c. 676–749) and is received in the Slavonic funeral rite.

The sticheron states the paradox the plate discusses: the human person is created in the image of God and is nevertheless disfigured in the grave, and this is a «mystery» ordained by God, not a defeat of the creator. The English translation is the atlas's own; it follows the Church Slavonic text, not a modern Russian translation.

notes.gloss: The one who has passed away; the departed.
Corruption, decay; the physical dissolution of the body.
